samples.summary: The one-shot `/start` link makes `wafflebase login` unrecoverable after any second request to it (reload, back-navigation, session restore, browser prefetch, or the user following the printed fallback URL)
samples.evidence: `startCallbackServer` serves `/start` exactly once: `if (startConsumed) { res.writeHead(410); ... }` and `startConsumed = true` is set before the 302 is even flushed (lines 272-279). `login` prints only that URL (`console.error(`Opening browser: ${startUrl}`)`, line 67) and also tells the user "If the browser does not open, visit the URL above" (line 68). But `open(startUrl)` (line 72) resolves as soon as the child process is spawned, not when navigation succeeds — so in the very case that instruction is written for (browser launched but the page never loaded, or the user reloads/goes back during the GitHub leg), the second request to `/start` returns 410 and the authorize URL is now unreachable: nothing else ever hands out the nonce-carrying URL. The callback then never arrives and the login dies at the 30 s timeout with the generic "Login timed out" message. There is no re-issue path and no separate way to print the authorize URL.

samples.summary: The timeout message re-introduces the very downgrade lever the nonce-less branch deliberately avoided: any local process can set `sawUnboundCallback` and thereby make a genuine timeout report "upgrade the server / use --allow-unbound-callback"
samples.evidence: Lines 306-317 refuse a nonce-less `/callback` and explicitly comment that ending the login there "would hand an attacker a downgrade lever", and the warning text is deliberately scrubbed of the flag name. But `sawUnboundCallback` is set by that same attacker-reachable branch, and at line 378 the timeout rejects with `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE`, which names `--allow-unbound-callback` and asserts the server is out of date. Any local process (or a page the browser visited) that sends a single `GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=x` before the real callback arrives — or simply while the user is slow at the GitHub prompt — makes a normal timeout or a genuinely failed login be misdiagnosed as version skew and steers the user at the flag that disables the binding. The state flag is never cleared even if a correctly-nonced callback would otherwise have been the outcome.

samples.summary: `normalizeCliState` is only reached when the port is also valid, so a malformed `cliState` with an out-of-range port is silently dropped — the docblock's "never a silent drop" invariant does not hold on that path
samples.evidence: `canActivate` nests `const nonce = normalizeCliState(cliState)` inside `if (Number.isInteger(portNum) && portNum >= 1024 && portNum <= 65535)` (lines 67-70). For `?mode=cli&port=80&cliState=<malformed>` no state token is minted, the request proceeds to GitHub with no state, and `githubAuthCallback` then takes the *web* branch (auth.controller.ts:145-149): it sets auth cookies in the browser and redirects to `FRONTEND_URL` for a request that plainly declared CLI mode, while the CLI's listener waits out its 30 s timeout. The docblock at lines 52-53 states "A present-but-malformed nonce is a 400 ..., never a silent drop", which is false for this path.

samples.summary: Several new `--dry-run` branches sit outside the action's try/catch, so a `seg()` throw bypasses the command's `outputError` envelope and escapes to the last-resort handler, unlike the sibling commands
samples.evidence: `docs get` (docs.ts:126-129), `sheets cells get` (cells.ts:21-33) and `tabs list` (tabs.ts:15-18) evaluate `seg(docId)`/`seg(tab)` in a dry-run branch placed *before* `try {`, whereas `notes get` (notes.ts:83), `slides get` (slides.ts:88) and `files get` (files.ts:114) place the identical branch inside the try. The new tests encode the divergence: `read-dry-run.test.ts` asserts `api-keys revoke .. --dry-run` sets `process.exitCode = 1` with an error envelope, but `docs get .. --dry-run` *rejects* the parse promise instead. Same user input, two different error shapes and exit paths from one CLI.

samples.summary: The `%2e` alternatives in `DOT_SEGMENT` are unreachable — the regex is tested against the already-`encodeURIComponent`-escaped value
samples.evidence: `DOT_SEGMENT = /^(?:\.|%2e){1,2}$/i` is applied at line 46 to `encoded = encodeURIComponent(value)`. `encodeURIComponent` escapes `%` to `%25`, so it can never emit the literal `%2e` the pattern is looking for; only the `\.` alternative can ever match. Harmless (the escaping makes the `%2e` forms inert as the docblock explains), but the branch is dead and the comment implies it is load-bearing.

finding.summary: The one-shot `/start` link makes `wafflebase login` unrecoverable after any second request to it (reload, back-navigation, session restore, browser prefetch, or the user following the printed fallback URL)
finding.evidence: `startCallbackServer` serves `/start` exactly once: `if (startConsumed) { res.writeHead(410); ... }` and `startConsumed = true` is set before the 302 is even flushed (lines 272-279). `login` prints only that URL (`console.error(`Opening browser: ${startUrl}`)`, line 67) and also tells the user "If the browser does not open, visit the URL above" (line 68). But `open(startUrl)` (line 72) resolves as soon as the child process is spawned, not when navigation succeeds — so in the very case that instruction is written for (browser launched but the page never loaded, or the user reloads/goes back during the GitHub leg), the second request to `/start` returns 410 and the authorize URL is now unreachable: nothing else ever hands out the nonce-carrying URL. The callback then never arrives and the login dies at the 30 s timeout with the generic "Login timed out" message. There is no re-issue path and no separate way to print the authorize URL.

verdict.reason: The cited code is present (login.ts:266-281 makes /start single-use; login.ts:66-72 prints only startUrl), but it is not a blocking correctness defect. (a) "Unrecoverable" is false: the 410 body is literally 'This one-time login link has already been opened. Re-run `wafflebase login`.' (login.ts:229-230) and the CLI's timeout error says 'Login timed out. Try again with `wafflebase login`.' (login.ts:380); re-running mints a fresh nonce/port (login.ts:46-50) and nothing is persisted before a successful exchange (login.ts:158-168) — no crash, no data loss, no corrupted state or broken invariant. (b) The single-use semantics are the specified, tested behavior, not a wrong condition or inverted logic: docs/design/cli.md:206-218 states "a second `GET /start` is answered `410` and hands out nothing … single use means it steals the nonce only by breaking the login visibly, never silently", asserted by the test 'hands the nonce out only once' (packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:208-223). Asking for a re-issue path or a separate way to print the authorize URL is a critique of that deliberate security tradeoff — design/security lens, not logic/runtime correctness. (c) Most named triggers do not actually re-request /start: it answers a bare 302 (login.ts:278), so the tab URL/history entry becomes the authorize URL and reload/session-restore refetch that, not /start; and the printed fallback URL only matters when no browser opened, in which case startConsumed is still false and the URL works — which is precisely the headless path line 68 addresses. What remains is a speculative prefetch/scanner double-fetch whose outcome is the two actionable messages above, i.e. a robustness/UX gap in an intentionally one-shot link.

finding.summary: The timeout message re-introduces the very downgrade lever the nonce-less branch deliberately avoided: any local process can set `sawUnboundCallback` and thereby make a genuine timeout report "upgrade the server / use --allow-unbound-callback"
finding.evidence: Lines 306-317 refuse a nonce-less `/callback` and explicitly comment that ending the login there "would hand an attacker a downgrade lever", and the warning text is deliberately scrubbed of the flag name. But `sawUnboundCallback` is set by that same attacker-reachable branch, and at line 378 the timeout rejects with `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE`, which names `--allow-unbound-callback` and asserts the server is out of date. Any local process (or a page the browser visited) that sends a single `GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=x` before the real callback arrives — or simply while the user is slow at the GitHub prompt — makes a normal timeout or a genuinely failed login be misdiagnosed as version skew and steers the user at the flag that disables the binding. The state flag is never cleared even if a correctly-nonced callback would otherwise have been the outcome.

verdict.reason: The code exists as described (login.ts:306-317 sets `sawUnboundCallback` from an attacker-reachable branch; login.ts:373-385 selects `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE` at the timeout), but it is not a blocking defect under the Correctness lens. (a) The only pure-correctness sub-claim — the flag is never cleared even when a correctly-nonced callback would have won — is inert: a valid callback sets `settled = true` (login.ts:367-370) and the entire timeout rejection is gated by `if (!settled)` (login.ts:374), with the caller additionally clearing the timer via `close()` in a `finally` (login.ts:81-83). A successful login can never surface the message. (b) Whenever the message is surfaced the login has genuinely failed (nothing valid arrived in 30s), so an error is thrown either way — no crash, no data loss, no lost state, no swallowed failure; nothing branches programmatically on the message text (only login.ts and the test reference the constant). The delta is diagnostic wording. (c) The substance of the finding — "attacker-reachable downgrade lever", "steers the user at the flag that disables the binding" — is a threat-model/social-engineering argument owned by the Security lens, which this lens is told to defer on; it is also the explicitly documented tradeoff (docs/design/rest-api.md:380: the nonce-less callback "is refused and reported, but does not end the login … Genuine skew, where nothing else arrives, ends with the version-skew message at the 30-second timeout").

finding.summary: `GET /start` is single-use and method-agnostic, so any duplicate/speculative request silently breaks the login for 30s
finding.evidence: `if (startConsumed) { res.writeHead(410) … }` at login.ts:272-276 marks the redirect consumed on the *first* request of any kind, before the browser has necessarily navigated. Real, non-adversarial duplicates exist: (a) a HEAD/preview/URL-scanner request (the handler never checks `req.method`, so HEAD consumes it), (b) omnibox/link prefetch when the user copy-pastes the printed `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/start` — the very headless path the comment at login.ts:52-65 says must keep working, (c) the user reloading or hitting Back and retrying after a hiccup, (d) a browser launcher that issues the URL twice. In all of these the real navigation gets `410 START_CONSUMED_MESSAGE`, no `/callback` ever arrives, and the CLI blocks the full 30s (login.ts:373-385) before failing with the generic `Login timed out` — with no hint that the one-time link was burnt. The previous code passed the authorize URL directly to `open()` and had no such failure mode, so this is a newly introduced hang/regression on ordinary paths.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described. login.ts:261 creates the handler without ever inspecting req.method, and the /start route sets `startConsumed = true` (line 277) on the first request of any kind before writing the 302 (278), with the second request answered `410 START_CONSUMED_MESSAGE` (272-276). No method filter, no re-arm, and no startConsumed-aware error path exists anywhere in the file. Once consumed, the real navigation never gets the authorize URL, no /callback arrives, `settled` stays false, and the only exit is the 30s setTimeout (373-385) whose message is refined solely by `sawUnboundCallback` — so the user waits the full timeout and sees the generic 'Login timed out' with no hint the one-time link was burnt. That directly contradicts the file's own stated invariant at 59-61 and docs/design/cli.md:217-218 that consumption 'breaks the login loudly/visibly'. The printed copy-paste URL (line 67 with startUrl from line 399) is the same single-use URL that packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:193-199 says the headless path depends on, so a single stray HEAD/prefetch/Back-refetch on it breaks login. Refutation grounds all fail: not-present (code is at the cited lines), already-guarded (no guard found — timeout bounds but does not prevent or explain it), out-of-scope (state flag flipped on the wrong event plus error handling that mis-reports a known failure as a generic timeout is squarely correctness, on the login core flow). Frequency of a duplicate request in real browsers is the only unresolved part, and uncertainty keeps the finding.

finding.summary: `sawUnboundCallback` lets any local process (or visited page) control the CLI's final error message, producing a false version-skew report
finding.evidence: `sawUnboundCallback` is set at login.ts:309-310 by *any* `GET /callback?code=…` with no `state`, which the surrounding comment itself notes is 'reachable by any local process or visited page'. The timeout then reports `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE` (login.ts:378-380) instead of 'Login timed out'. So a stray/hostile nonce-less request during an otherwise ordinary timeout (browser never finished, network hiccup) makes the CLI assert the *server* is out of date and instruct the user to re-run with `--allow-unbound-callback` — the exact downgrade steer the comment at login.ts:298-305 claims to have closed; it is merely deferred to the timeout. The error is factually wrong on a path where the server is perfectly current.

verdict.reason: The code is present as described: login.ts:306-317 sets `sawUnboundCallback` from any nonce-less `GET /callback`, and login.ts:373-385 substitutes UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE for the timeout message. But it is not a blocking defect under the correctness lens. (a) No correctness impact on the flow: the nonce-less branch only flips a reporting flag and returns 400 — it never touches `settled`/`callbackResolve`, the real callback still wins (verified by login-callback.test.ts:92-119), and the login in the described scenario was already failing by timeout regardless. No crash, data loss, dropped await, or broken invariant; only the wording of an error on an already-failed path changes, and the user has already seen the accurate stderr warning emitted at login.ts:311-314. (b) The behavior is the explicit written specification, not an oversight: docs/design/cli.md:229-237 and docs/design/rest-api.md:380 both state that the nonce-less callback must not abort the login and that the version-skew message replaces the timeout message at 30s, naming the abort alternative as the worse (downgrade-lever) option. (c) The harm the finding actually argues — an attacker-triggerable nudge toward `--allow-unbound-callback` — is a security/social-engineering concern, explicitly out of this lens ("Security (its own lens)"). Grep confirms `sawUnboundCallback` has no other reader (only login.ts:248,309,310,378), so the divergence is cosmetic in every path. Residual issue is at most a nit-level diagnostic-attribution gap, not major/blocking.
